analysis.one_liner: Makes drug companies give the patent office the same claims they give the FDA, and punishes non-disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee action or vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, after drawing only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require drug companies to share with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office the same information they submit to the FDA when seeking drug approval, and to certify the two sets of statements match [S2]. It also lets generic drug makers use a company's failure to disclose that information as a defense in patent lawsuits, and lets the FDA refuse or delay approval if a sponsor breaks the rules [S2]. The aim is to stop companies from telling the patent office one thing and the FDA another, which can extend monopoly protection and keep generic competition off the market [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Future generic and biosimilar manufacturers and their potential customers: the bill requires brand-name drug makers to share with the patent office the same data and arguments they give the FDA, and to certify the two filings match, which would make it harder to obtain or defend patents built on inconsistent statements [S2]. Generic and biosimilar challengers would also gain a new court defense against patents whose owners failed to disclose required information [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug companies to certify that statements they made to the patent office about their drugs' data and prior art match what they told the FDA, closing a gap that lets the same fact be described differently to each agency [S2].

Gives generic and biosimilar makers a court defense against a drug patent if its owner negligently or intentionally failed to disclose required information, weakening patents obtained through one-sided arguments [S2].
Lets the FDA refuse approval if a sponsor fails to certify consistent disclosures, and makes non-compliance a prohibited act subject to FDA enforcement [S2].
Targets practices that can stretch drug monopolies beyond what the underlying invention deserves, which is one of the reasons brand-name drugs stay expensive after patents should have expired [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face new disclosure duties, risk FDA approval delays for non-compliance, and a new defense against patent infringement suits if they withheld information from either agency [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill never received any committee hearing, markup, or vote in either chamber, so its workability, costs, and effects on the patent system were never publicly examined [S4].

The threat of FDA disapproval or delay for disclosure missteps could give the agency leverage to pressure drug sponsors on matters unrelated to patent integrity, and compliance disputes could entangle the approval process [S2].

The non-disclosure defense applies even to negligent (not just intentional) failures to disclose, which could expose valid patents to invalidation over paperwork errors and increase litigation for all sides [S2].

Reduced patent certainty for brand-name drugs could, under industry arguments, weaken incentives to invest in developing new medicines — an objection supporters would need to answer with evidence the bill never got a hearing to test [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary Americans, the potential benefit is real but indirect and gradual: patents that were obtained or defended using inconsistent statements between the FDA and the patent office could be challenged more easily, letting generic and biosimilar competition bring prices down sooner [S2]. The costs fall almost entirely on brand-name drug companies in the form of new disclosure duties, possible FDA enforcement, and a new litigation defense against their patents [S2]. The main honest caveat is that the bill was never examined in a hearing or markup, so nobody assessed how it would work in practice, how the FDA would enforce it, or whether negligent-disclosure defenses would chill legitimate patenting [S4]. On balance it is a modest, targeted anti-abuse measure whose cost to the public is close to zero and whose benefit depends entirely on how often the targeted behavior occurs — and it was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees from the day it was introduced, was never taken up, and died when the 118th Congress ended [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Ann Kuster introduced the bill on September 13, 2023, joined by Republican Rep. Diane Harshbarger as an original cosponsor [S2][S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees the same day, and on September 15, 2023 it went to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee [S1][S4].
No further action followed: neither committee held a markup, and the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].
Aside from the original cosponsor, the bill attracted only one additional cosponsor over its entire life [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: their current practice of arguing drug facts differently before the FDA and the patent office continues unchanged, because the bill that would have required consistent disclosure never received committee consideration. Generic and biosimilar makers, and patients waiting on cheaper competition, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Generic and biosimilar makers, not patients

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in either committee, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew one cosponsor from the opposing party and no committee or floor action ever split along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would burden them with new disclosure duties to the patent office, expose them to FDA enforcement and patent-infringement defenses, and potentially shorten or weaken patent protection that sustains high drug prices. Because the bill died without a vote, their interests are unaffected.
A non-disclosure defense and consistent FDA-patent disclosures would give them a new tool to challenge patents that block generic and biosimilar entry.
